subject: HEALTH
overview: Plan about 20 minutes a day: a short reading or video, a hands-on activity (label reading, role-play, charting), and a quick check question. Lessons build the eight California health skills, so keep asking 'Which skill are we using?' and have your child apply it to real family situations. Preview sensitive units first — puberty and reproduction (weeks 17–23) and alcohol, tobacco and other drugs (weeks 24–33) — and honor your family's values; California law lets parents opt out of sexual health instruction. Keep a calm, matter-of-fact tone, use correct terms, and welcome questions (the anonymous question box helps).

weeks.prep: Get a health journal and markers. Print or write the eight California health education standards (essential concepts, analyzing influences, accessing valid information, interpersonal communication, decision making, goal setting, practicing health-enhancing behaviors, health promotion/advocacy). Prepare a bedtime-vs-video-game scenario card.
misconceptions: Thinking health only means not being sick. Health has physical, mental/emotional and social sides, and all three affect each other.
Writing vague goals ('eat better'). A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

days.guide: Draw a triangle labeled physical, mental/emotional and social. Your child lists three current habits on each side and stars the strongest side; ask how a weak side affects the others.

questions.q: Name the three sides of the wellness triangle and give a habit for each.
questions.a: Physical (e.g., sleeping 9–10 hours), mental/emotional (e.g., journaling when upset), social (e.g., playing with friends, getting along with family).

days.guide: Read the list of health skills together. Your child matches each skill to a real example (e.g., 'reading a cereal label' = accessing valid information).

questions.q: Which health skill is it when you ask your doctor whether a vitamin is safe?
questions.a: Accessing valid information (also uses communication).

days.guide: Teach the 5 steps, then walk through the scenario: it's bedtime but you want to finish a level. Your child lists options and consequences aloud before deciding.

questions.q: List the five decision steps in order.
questions.a: 1) State the problem 2) List options 3) Weigh consequences 4) Decide and act 5) Evaluate the result.

days.guide: Explain SMART. Your child writes one health goal for the month and makes a tracking chart with boxes for each day.

questions.q: Make 'drink more water' a SMART goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will drink water instead of soda at lunch 5 days a week for the next 4 weeks and check off each day on my chart.'

days.guide: Your child teaches you the triangle and decision steps, then answers a 6-question quick check orally or on paper.

questions.q: Why should you evaluate your decision at the end?
questions.a: To learn whether it worked out and what you'd do differently next time.

weeks.assessment_key: Quick check answers: 1) Physical, mental/emotional, social 2) Example habit for each side 3) Decision steps: problem, options, consequences, decide, evaluate 4) SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound 5) A health skill example such as reading labels = accessing information 6) Health sides affect each other (e.g., poor sleep → grumpy → arguments). SMART goal chart rubric: 4 = all five SMART parts plus a daily tracking chart; 3 = missing one part; 2 = vague goal; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Get butcher paper (or tape printer paper together), markers, a stopwatch and a ruler. Preview the KidsHealth article on the endocrine system ('Your Endocrine System' for kids).
misconceptions: Thinking each body system works alone. Systems constantly work together — e.g., running uses muscles, bones, nerves, heart and lungs at once.
Thinking blood vessels and the heart are part of the respiratory system. They are the circulatory system; the respiratory system is the airways and lungs.

days.guide: Trace your child's body. They sketch and label major bones (skull, ribs, spine, femur), a few muscles (biceps, quadriceps, heart muscle) and the heart with main blood vessels.

questions.q: What is the job of the skeletal system?
questions.a: Support the body, protect organs (skull protects brain, ribs protect heart and lungs), and work with muscles to move; bones also make blood cells.

days.guide: Take resting pulse, 2 minutes of jumping jacks, retake. Your child explains what the heart and lungs did.

questions.q: Why did your breathing and pulse both speed up?
questions.a: Muscles needed more oxygen and had more carbon dioxide to remove, so the lungs breathed faster and the heart pumped faster to carry oxygen in the blood.

days.guide: Hold a ruler at the 30 cm mark above your child's open fingers; drop it without warning 5 times and record where they catch it.

questions.q: Which systems worked together to catch the ruler?
questions.a: Nervous system (eyes send signal to brain, brain sends signal through nerves) and muscular system (hand muscles close).

days.guide: Read the endocrine article. Your child adds the pituitary (base of brain), thyroid (front of neck) and adrenal glands (on top of the kidneys) to the body map.

questions.q: What do glands of the endocrine system make, and how do they travel?
questions.a: Hormones — chemical messengers carried in the bloodstream.

days.guide: Your child explains how three systems work during running, then labels a blank diagram. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: When you run, how do the muscular, circulatory and respiratory systems work together?
questions.a: Muscles move bones; lungs take in oxygen; the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to muscles and carries away carbon dioxide.

weeks.assessment_key: Body map: correctly placed and labeled skeletal (skull, ribs, spine, femur), muscular (biceps, quadriceps), circulatory (heart, arteries/veins), endocrine (pituitary, thyroid, adrenals). Labeling quiz: brain, heart, lungs, pituitary (base of brain), thyroid (neck), adrenals (top of kidneys), femur (thigh), ribs (chest). Proficient = 80% correct and an accurate 'running' explanation linking three systems.

weeks.prep: Collect baby/childhood photos and any recorded heights (doctor records, growth chart, doorframe). Pick one health topic (e.g., sunscreen) and find a .gov page, a product ad and a social-media post about it. Write a 4-question reliability checklist: Who wrote it? Are they an expert? Are they selling something? Is it current and supported by evidence?
misconceptions: Believing information is true because it's online or has many likes. Check who wrote it, their expertise, purpose and date.
Thinking ads are neutral information. Ads are written to sell a product.

days.guide: Your child builds a timeline with photos, heights and skills gained (walking, reading, riding a bike).

questions.q: Name a skill you gained in early childhood and one in middle childhood.
questions.a: Example: walking/talking (early); reading chapter books, riding a bike (middle).

days.guide: Make a 5-column chart: infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, older adulthood with ages and main changes.

questions.q: What stage begins with puberty?
questions.a: Adolescence (roughly ages 10–19).

days.guide: Apply the checklist to the three sources and rank them. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why is a .gov page usually more reliable than a product ad?
questions.a: Government health sites are written by experts, reviewed, and not trying to sell a product; ads aim to persuade you to buy.

days.guide: Your child lists four trusted adults (parent, doctor, school nurse, relative) and two valid sources (e.g., KidsHealth.org, CDC.gov). Discuss together.

questions.q: What makes an adult 'trusted'?
questions.a: They are safe, care about you, listen, give accurate help, and you can go to them with problems.

days.guide: Sort 8 source cards as reliable or unreliable, then write a paragraph on how to check health information.

questions.q: A website selling a 'miracle vitamin' says it cures colds. Reliable? Why?
questions.a: No — it is trying to sell, makes an unsupported claim, and isn't from a medical expert.

weeks.assessment_key: Source sort: reliable — government (.gov) health agencies, major children's hospitals and medical organizations, KidsHealth, a doctor/school nurse; unreliable — product ads, anonymous social-media posts, sites selling 'cures,' undated blogs. Paragraph rubric: 4 = names at least three checks (author/expertise, purpose/selling, evidence, date) and a trusted adult; 3 = two checks; 2 = one; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Print MyPlate (MyPlate.gov / MyPlate Kids' Place) and gather food magazines or grocery flyers, scissors and glue. Use the MyPlate Plan tool to get amounts for your child's age, sex and activity level.
misconceptions: Thinking fat is always bad. The body needs some fat (especially unsaturated) for energy and to absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
Forgetting water is a nutrient. Water is essential for every body process.

days.guide: Your child makes a 6-panel chart with each nutrient's job and two foods. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is the main job of carbohydrates and of protein?
questions.a: Carbohydrates are the body's main energy source; protein builds and repairs tissues like muscle.

days.guide: Read about calcium (bones), iron (carries oxygen in blood), and protein (growth) during growth spurts; list rich foods.

questions.q: Name two foods rich in calcium and two rich in iron.
questions.a: Calcium: milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy milk, broccoli. Iron: lean meat, beans, spinach, fortified cereal.

days.guide: Use MyPlate to look up daily amounts and record them. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Which food group should fill about half the plate?
questions.a: Fruits and vegetables.

days.guide: Build a balanced plate collage from magazine pictures. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why is variety important on MyPlate?
questions.a: Different foods provide different nutrients, so variety helps you get all you need.

days.guide: Give the 10-question quiz; your child explains the collage. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Which nutrient helps digestion and is found in whole grains, beans and vegetables?
questions.a: Fiber (a type of carbohydrate).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) carbohydrates — energy 2) protein — build/repair 3) fats — stored energy, vitamin absorption 4) vitamins — help body processes 5) minerals — e.g., calcium for bones 6) water — temperature, transport 7) calcium foods: dairy 8) iron foods: meat, beans 9) half plate: fruits & veg 10) fiber sources: whole grains, beans. Collage: all five groups with vegetables and fruits ≈ half the plate, grains (half whole), protein, dairy.

weeks.prep: Collect labels from soda, juice, sports drink, chocolate milk and water; sugar or sand and a teaspoon. Gather labels for canned soup, chips, crackers and a fresh/frozen vegetable. Key fact: 4 grams of sugar ≈ 1 teaspoon.
misconceptions: Thinking 100% juice has no sugar. It has natural sugar and is less filling than whole fruit; whole fruit is a better choice.
Reading % Daily Value as a percentage of the food. %DV shows how much of a day's recommended amount one serving provides.

days.guide: Your child finds grams of sugar on each label, divides by 4 to get teaspoons, and measures that many teaspoons into cups.

questions.q: A 12-oz soda has 39 g of sugar. How many teaspoons is that?
questions.a: About 10 teaspoons (39 ÷ 4 ≈ 9.75).

days.guide: Rank the four foods by sodium per serving. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Which usually has the least sodium: canned soup, chips, crackers or fresh vegetables?
questions.a: Fresh vegetables.

days.guide: Sort food cards: unsaturated (olive oil, nuts, avocado, fish) vs. saturated (butter, fatty meat, cheese).

questions.q: Why are plant oils and nuts better choices than butter?
questions.a: They're mostly unsaturated fats, which are better for heart health than saturated fat.

days.guide: Teach 5/20: 5% DV or less is low; 20% DV or more is high. Apply to 4 labels. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: A snack has 22% DV sodium. Is that high or low?
questions.a: High (20% or more).

days.guide: Complete the worksheet and write three swaps. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Give a swap that cuts added sugar.
questions.a: Water or plain milk instead of soda; whole fruit instead of fruit snacks.

weeks.assessment_key: Label worksheet: teaspoons calculated as grams ÷ 4; correctly labels nutrients low (≤5% DV) or high (≥20% DV); identifies saturated vs. unsaturated fats. Swaps: three realistic substitutions (e.g., water for soda, fresh veggies for chips, unsalted nuts for crackers).

weeks.prep: Collect 5 cereal boxes and a measuring cup. Print a blank Nutrition Facts label for labeling. Review names for sugar: sucrose, corn syrup, high-fructose corn syrup, dextrose, cane juice, honey, molasses.
misconceptions: Thinking the label amounts are for the whole box. Amounts are per serving; multiply if you eat more.
Thinking 'wheat flour' means whole grain. Look for the word 'whole' (whole wheat, whole grain oats).

days.guide: Your child labels each part: serving size, servings per container, calories, %DV, nutrients to limit, nutrients to get more of, footnote.

questions.q: Where should you look first on a Nutrition Facts label?
questions.a: The serving size and servings per container.

days.guide: Pour a usual bowl of cereal, measure it, compare to serving size and recalculate sugar. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Serving size is 1 cup with 12 g sugar. You eat 2 cups. How much sugar?
questions.a: 24 g (about 6 teaspoons).

days.guide: Read ingredient lists, which are in order by weight (most first); circle whole grains and sugars.

questions.q: What does it mean if sugar is the first ingredient?
questions.a: There is more sugar by weight than any other ingredient.

days.guide: Compare 5 cereals for fiber, sugar and sodium; use the decision steps to choose. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Which cereal is healthiest: high fiber/low sugar or low fiber/high sugar?
questions.a: High fiber and low added sugar.

days.guide: Give a test with two unfamiliar products. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: A label says 2.5 servings per container. If you eat the whole container with 150 calories per serving, how many calories?
questions.a: 375 calories.

weeks.assessment_key: Label test: correctly identifies serving size, calories, %DV, nutrients to limit (saturated fat, sodium, added sugars), nutrients to get more of (fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, potassium), recalculates for a different portion, names whole grains and sugars in ingredients. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather yogurt, fruit, granola, vegetables and hummus for Wednesday; make 20 snack cards (apple, cheese stick, chips, candy bar, carrots, crackers, nuts, cookies, popcorn, fruit snacks, etc.). Find a short kids' article on breakfast and school performance (e.g., KidsHealth 'Break for Breakfast').
misconceptions: Thinking skipping breakfast saves time with no cost. Without breakfast, energy and concentration drop by mid-morning.
Thinking all snacks are 'junk.' Nutrient-dense snacks (fruit, yogurt, nuts, veggies) help growing bodies; 'sometimes' foods give empty calories.
Thinking you only need water when thirsty. Drink regularly through the day and more when active or hot.

days.guide: Read the article; your child plans three quick breakfasts, each with at least three food groups (e.g., whole-grain toast + peanut butter + banana).

questions.q: Why does breakfast help you at school?
questions.a: It refuels the body and brain after the night, giving energy to concentrate, remember and stay alert.

days.guide: Your child sorts snack cards into everyday vs. sometimes and justifies with nutrients (fiber, protein, added sugar, sodium).

questions.q: Why is a cheese stick an everyday snack but fruit snacks a sometimes snack?
questions.a: Cheese gives protein and calcium; fruit snacks are mostly added sugar with few nutrients (empty calories).

days.guide: Wash hands, then your child makes a parfait or veggie-and-hummus plate and records food groups.

questions.q: What food groups are in a yogurt parfait with berries and granola?
questions.a: Dairy (yogurt), fruit (berries), grains (granola).

days.guide: Your child tracks every drink for a day and designs a reminder chart (e.g., a bottle with time markings).

questions.q: Name two signs you need more water.
questions.a: Thirst, dark yellow urine, headache, tiredness or dizziness.

days.guide: Your child writes a one-week snack menu and justifies three choices using label data (fiber, added sugar, protein, %DV).

questions.q: What does 'nutrient-dense' mean?
questions.a: A food with lots of vitamins, minerals, fiber or protein for its calories.

weeks.assessment_key: Snack menu rubric: 4 = 7 days of mostly nutrient-dense snacks across several food groups, three justifications citing specific label numbers (e.g., '5 g fiber, 0 g added sugar'); 3 = justifications general; 2 = mostly 'sometimes' foods or no justification; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print a one-day food log (columns: time, food/drink, amount, food group) and gather grocery flyers. Set a realistic one-day budget with your child. Plan which meal you'll cook together on Thursday and buy ingredients; review knife safety (claw grip, cut away from body, cutting board on a damp towel).
misconceptions: Thinking a balanced day must be expensive. Beans, eggs, oats, bananas, frozen vegetables and canned fish are low-cost and nutritious.
Forgetting drinks in a food log. Beverages (juice, soda, milk) count toward sugar and food groups.

days.guide: Your child logs everything eaten and drunk for a day, including amounts, by food group. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why record amounts and not just foods?
questions.a: To compare with MyPlate's recommended amounts (cups, ounces) and see if you got enough or too much.

days.guide: Compare the log with MyPlate recommendations; highlight over and under groups. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: MyPlate says 2½ cups of vegetables and you had 1 cup. How much more do you need?
questions.a: 1½ cups.

days.guide: Your child plans three meals and two snacks within the budget using flyer prices. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Name two inexpensive protein foods.
questions.a: Any two: dried or canned beans, eggs, peanut butter, canned tuna, lentils.

days.guide: Cook the planned meal together: wash hands 20 seconds with soap, use the claw grip, separate raw meat from produce.

questions.q: Why keep raw meat away from vegetables you'll eat raw?
questions.a: Raw meat can carry germs (like Salmonella or E. coli) that can spread to other food (cross-contamination).

days.guide: Your child presents the plan, then takes the unit test. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What does MyPlate recommend about grains?
questions.a: Make at least half of your grains whole grains.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test answer key: 1) six nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water 2) fruits and vegetables fill half the plate 3) 5% DV low / 20% DV high 4) 4 g sugar ≈ 1 teaspoon 5) check serving size first 6) ingredients listed by weight, most first 7) calcium builds bones; iron carries oxygen 8) choose water/milk over sugary drinks 9) wash hands 20 seconds 10) avoid cross-contamination. Meal plan rubric: 4 = meets MyPlate amounts for all groups, within budget, variety, clear presentation; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = major groups missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a stopwatch, a yardstick taped to a box for sit-and-reach, a mat, and a fitness log. Measure a walk/run route so distance can be estimated (laps of a known loop).
misconceptions: Thinking being thin means being fit. Fitness is about the five components, not appearance.
Thinking flexibility doesn't matter. It helps prevent injury and allows full movement.

days.guide: Teach the five components and have your child match an activity to each (jogging, push-ups, plank, stretching).

questions.q: Which component is improved by swimming laps for 20 minutes?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance.

days.guide: Time a 10-minute walk/run; record distance and heart rate at the end. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What does a faster heart rate recovery after exercise show?
questions.a: Better cardiorespiratory fitness.

days.guide: Count curl-ups and push-ups in 30 seconds each, using good form. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Is doing many curl-ups strength or endurance?
questions.a: Muscular endurance — doing a movement many times.

days.guide: Sit-and-reach with the yardstick; record best of three reaching slowly without bouncing. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Why reach slowly instead of bouncing?
questions.a: Bouncing can strain or tear muscles; slow reaching is safer and gives a truer measure.

days.guide: Chart baselines and write one goal per component. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Write a goal for flexibility.
questions.a: Example: 'Improve my sit-and-reach by 2 inches in 6 weeks by stretching 5 minutes after activity 4 days a week.'

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline chart: all five components recorded (walk/run distance and heart rate, curl-ups, push-ups, sit-and-reach; body composition discussed only as a concept — do not weigh or measure body fat). Goals rubric: 4 = a SMART goal for each measured component; 3 = most components; 2 = vague goals; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather a calendar and jump rope; plan music for dancing. Learn the guidelines: kids 6–17 need 60+ minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week each.
misconceptions: Thinking the 60 minutes must be done all at once. It can be added up across the day.
Thinking screen time is harmless if you're sitting quietly. Long sedentary time cuts into activity and sleep.

days.guide: Read about benefits; your child lists five (stronger heart and bones, better sleep, better mood, less stress, better focus, healthy weight).

questions.q: Name three benefits of regular physical activity.
questions.a: Any three: stronger heart and lungs, stronger bones and muscles, better sleep, improved mood, lower stress, better concentration.

days.guide: Try walking, jumping rope and dancing for 3 minutes each; use the talk test. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: How does the talk test tell moderate from vigorous?
questions.a: Moderate: you can talk but not sing. Vigorous: you can only say a few words before needing a breath.

days.guide: Create a 7-day plan of 60+ minutes daily with muscle- and bone-strengthening 3 days. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Name a bone-strengthening activity.
questions.a: Jumping rope, running, hopscotch, basketball — activities with impact.

days.guide: Track screen time for a day and plan two active swaps. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Give an active swap for 30 minutes of video games.
questions.a: A bike ride, shooting hoops, or a dance video.

days.guide: Do day one of the plan; take the guidelines quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: How many minutes of activity do kids need daily?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 60 minutes daily 2) moderate = can talk, not sing 3) vigorous = few words 4) muscle-strengthening 3 days/week (push-ups, climbing) 5) bone-strengthening 3 days/week (jumping, running). Plan rubric: 4 = 60+ minutes every day with intensity labeled and strength/bone activities on 3+ days; 3 = small gaps; 2 = under 60 minutes most days; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Get your child's bike helmet and water bottle. Check the heat index if exercising outdoors. Prepare a points chart template.
misconceptions: Thinking a helmet just needs to be on your head. It must fit: level on the forehead (two fingers above eyebrows), straps form a V under each ear, chin strap snug (one finger).
Waiting until thirsty to drink in heat. Drink before, during and after activity.

days.guide: Role-play asking for a family walk: use a clear, respectful request with a reason and a specific time ('Could we walk to the park after dinner? I want to reach my activity goal.').

questions.q: What makes a request clear and respectful?
questions.a: Calm tone, eye contact, a specific request and reason, and listening to the answer.

days.guide: List safety rules for heat, hydration, sun and protective gear; check helmet fit with the 2-V-1 rule.

questions.q: Describe the 2-V-1 helmet check.
questions.a: Two fingers above the eyebrows, straps form a V under each ear, one finger fits under the chin strap.

days.guide: Design a one-week family activity challenge with points. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why might a family challenge help you reach goals?
questions.a: It adds support, fun and accountability.

days.guide: Retest one baseline from week 9 and compare. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: If push-ups went from 8 to 11, how much improvement?
questions.a: 3 more push-ups.

days.guide: Write a reflection on goal progress; take the fitness quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Name two signs of heat illness.
questions.a: Dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps, heavy sweating or confusion.

weeks.assessment_key: Fitness quiz key: 1) five components 2) 60 minutes 3) talk test 4) helmet 2-V-1 5) heat illness signs and action (stop, shade, water, tell adult). Reflection rubric: 4 = compares data, explains why, and sets next step; 3 = compares data; 2 = general; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Have the health journal ready. Read the KidsHealth article on dieting for kids ahead of time. Model positive talk about bodies at home this week. Watch for signs of serious body worries (skipping meals, intense exercise, negative self-talk) and talk with your pediatrician if you see them.
misconceptions: Thinking there is one 'right' body type. Healthy bodies come in many shapes and sizes, largely shaped by genetics.
Thinking dieting is healthy for kids. Growing bodies need regular balanced meals; restrictive dieting can harm growth and energy.

days.guide: Discuss body image; your child writes three things their body lets them do. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is body image?
questions.a: How you see, think and feel about your body.

days.guide: Look at family photos to notice inherited traits; list factors affecting size (genetics, growth stage, activity, nutrition).

questions.q: Name two factors that affect body size.
questions.a: Genetics and growth stage (also nutrition, activity, sleep).

days.guide: Read about dieting; list harms of skipping meals and fad diets. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why are fad diets harmful for kids?
questions.a: They cut out nutrients needed for growth, lower energy and focus, and can lead to unhealthy eating patterns.

days.guide: Replace body-shaming comments in 5 scenarios with respectful ones. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Replace: 'You're too skinny to play.'
questions.a: 'Come play with us!' — or say nothing about bodies and focus on the person.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on healthy body image and answer the check. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How can you build a positive body image?
questions.a: Focus on what your body can do, avoid comparing, use kind self-talk, and limit media that makes you feel bad.

weeks.assessment_key: Quick check: 1) body image = how you see/feel about your body 2) genetics shapes body type 3) dieting harms growing kids 4) respectful alternative 5) one strategy for positive body image. Paragraph rubric: 4 = defines body image, explains genetics/diversity, gives two strategies; 3 = one strategy; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather magazines or catalogs, and preview online: a short photo-retouching video (e.g., Dove 'Evolution') and two kids' food commercials. Make a list of the 6 advertising techniques with definitions. Gather art supplies for the counter-ad.
misconceptions: Thinking photos in ads and social media show real bodies. Most are posed, lit, filtered and digitally edited.
Thinking ads are made to inform. Ads are made to sell; they highlight what's appealing and leave out what isn't.
Thinking advertising doesn't affect you. Repeated messages shape what we want and how we see ourselves, even when we know they're ads.

days.guide: Explain the 6 techniques: bandwagon (everyone has it), celebrity endorsement, fun/excitement, health claims, giveaways/prizes, beautiful people. Your child finds and labels one example of each in magazines.

questions.q: An ad shows a famous athlete drinking a sports drink. Which technique is that?
questions.a: Celebrity endorsement (testimonial).

days.guide: Watch the retouching video; discuss what changed (skin smoothed, neck lengthened, eyes enlarged) and how it might make viewers feel.

questions.q: How can edited images affect people's body image?
questions.a: They create unrealistic standards that no real body matches, which can make people feel bad about their own bodies.

days.guide: Watch two kids' food commercials; your child fills in: target audience, techniques used, and what the ad leaves out (sugar, nutrition, price).

questions.q: Who is the target audience of a cereal ad with cartoon characters and a toy prize, and what's left out?
questions.a: Young children; it leaves out nutrition facts like high added sugar and low fiber.

days.guide: Compare ads aimed at boys vs. girls (toys or clothing); list stereotypes about bodies and behaviors.

questions.q: Give an example of a gender stereotype in ads and why it's unfair.
questions.a: Example: boys shown only as muscular and tough, girls only as thin and pretty — it limits how kids think they should look or act.

days.guide: Your child creates a counter-ad promoting healthy body image or an honest healthy food, and labels the technique it uses or answers.

questions.q: What makes a counter-ad honest?
questions.a: It uses real, unedited images and true, accurate information, and doesn't make exaggerated claims.

weeks.assessment_key: Counter-ad rubric: 4 = clear health-enhancing message, honest images and claims, names the advertising technique it uses or counters and explains it in 2–3 sentences; 3 = message plus technique named; 2 = message unclear or technique missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather samples or photos of deodorant and antiperspirant labels, gentle face wash, shampoo and nail clippers. Preview KidsHealth articles on body odor and acne.
misconceptions: Thinking acne comes from being dirty or eating chocolate. Acne comes mainly from hormones making oil glands more active; pores clog with oil and dead skin. Scrubbing hard makes it worse.
Thinking deodorant and antiperspirant are the same. Deodorant fights odor; antiperspirant reduces sweat.

days.guide: Explain that in puberty hormones make sweat and oil glands more active; bacteria breaking down sweat cause body odor, and oil clogging pores causes acne.

questions.q: What actually causes body odor?
questions.a: Bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat (especially from glands in the armpits and groin).

days.guide: Read about gentle washing and acne myths; your child writes a morning and evening routine.

questions.q: Should you scrub your face hard to stop pimples? Why?
questions.a: No — scrubbing irritates skin and can make acne worse; wash gently twice a day with mild cleanser.

days.guide: Compare labels: antiperspirants list aluminum compounds as the active ingredient. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What's the difference between deodorant and antiperspirant?
questions.a: Deodorant reduces odor (covers scent, fights bacteria); antiperspirant reduces sweating (usually with aluminum compounds). Many products are both.

days.guide: Discuss washing hair more often as it gets oily; practice trimming nails straight across. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why trim toenails straight across?
questions.a: To help prevent ingrown toenails.

days.guide: Build a personal hygiene checklist and take the myth-or-fact quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Myth or fact: you only need to shower when you look dirty.
questions.a: Myth — during puberty, daily showers (especially after exercise) prevent odor even if you don't look dirty.

weeks.assessment_key: Myth/fact key: Acne is caused by dirt — myth; Puberty makes sweat glands more active — fact; Deodorant stops sweating — myth (antiperspirant reduces sweat); Popping pimples helps them heal — myth; Washing face gently twice daily helps — fact; Shower after exercise — fact. Checklist: daily shower, deodorant, face wash AM/PM, clean clothes, hair washing, nail care, brushing teeth. Proficient = 80% on quiz and complete checklist.

weeks.prep: Get a new toothbrush, floss, a 2-minute timer, and disclosing tablets (pharmacy) or dark grape juice. Find your child's last dental and medical check-up records.
misconceptions: Thinking brushing once a day is enough. Brush twice a day for two minutes and floss once daily.
Thinking sugar itself eats teeth. Plaque bacteria eat sugar and make acid that dissolves enamel.

days.guide: Chew a disclosing tablet to show plaque; brush 2 minutes with small circles at the gumline, then recheck.

questions.q: What is plaque?
questions.a: A sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth.

days.guide: Practice flossing: 18 inches, wrap around middle fingers, C-shape around each tooth, gently below the gumline.

questions.q: How do sugar and plaque cause cavities?
questions.a: Plaque bacteria feed on sugar and produce acid that dissolves tooth enamel, making holes (cavities).

days.guide: Your child interviews you about the last check-ups and lists what was checked (teeth cleaning, X-rays, height, weight, vision, vaccines).

questions.q: Why have check-ups when you feel fine?
questions.a: To catch problems early, track growth, and keep vaccines up to date.

days.guide: Read about braces (straighten teeth/jaw alignment by an orthodontist) and mouth guards (contact sports).

questions.q: When should you wear a mouth guard?
questions.a: In contact sports or activities where your mouth could be hit (football, basketball, martial arts, skateboarding).

days.guide: Make a dental poster and answer 5 questions. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How does fluoride help teeth?
questions.a: It strengthens enamel, making teeth more resistant to acid and cavities.

weeks.assessment_key: Oral health answers: 1) brush twice a day for 2 minutes 2) floss once a day 3) plaque = sticky bacteria film 4) bacteria + sugar → acid → cavity 5) fluoride strengthens enamel. Poster rubric: 4 = accurate brushing, flossing, diet and check-up tips with visuals; 3 = 3 of 4; 2 = 2; 1 = 1 or fewer.

weeks.prep: Print a 4-night sleep log (bedtime, screen-off time, wake time, total hours, how I felt). Know the recommendation: children 6–12 need 9–12 hours of sleep per night.
misconceptions: Thinking you can 'catch up' on sleep only on weekends. Regular sleep schedules work best.
Thinking screens right before bed help you relax. Screen light and stimulating content can delay sleep.

days.guide: Read about sleep; your child lists four effects of too little sleep. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name four effects of too little sleep.
questions.a: Any four: trouble concentrating, poor memory, grumpiness/mood swings, slower reaction time, more illness, less energy for activity.

days.guide: Start the 4-night sleep log. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How many hours should a 10-year-old sleep?
questions.a: 9–12 hours per night.

days.guide: Design a 30-minute screen-free wind-down routine. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Give two wind-down activities.
questions.a: Reading, a warm shower, journaling, quiet music, stretching.

days.guide: Combine hygiene, dental care, sleep and activity into a daily routine chart. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why does a routine help health?
questions.a: Habits become automatic, so healthy behaviors happen consistently.

days.guide: Analyze the sleep log, set a goal, and take the unit quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What hormone is released during deep sleep that helps you grow?
questions.a: Growth hormone.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit quiz: 1) sweat/oil glands more active in puberty 2) deodorant vs antiperspirant 3) brush 2×2 min, floss daily 4) plaque + sugar → acid 5) 9–12 hours sleep 6) growth hormone in sleep 7) screens delay sleep. Routine chart rubric: 4 = includes hygiene, dental, sleep schedule and activity; 3 = 3 areas; 2 = 2; 1 = 1.

weeks.prep: Gather the parent letter/unit outline for weeks 17–23, a box with a slot for anonymous questions, slips of paper, and the AMAZE.org video 'Puberty: Some Changes to Expect' (or similar). Find your child's past heights (doctor records or growth chart). PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking puberty happens at the same age for everyone. It can begin anywhere from about age 8 to 14 and still be completely normal.
Thinking puberty only happens to girls (or only to boys). Everyone goes through puberty; some changes are shared and some differ.

days.guide: Sit together and look over the unit outline and materials so nothing is a surprise. Explain the question box: any question, no names, answered honestly. Say clearly that questions are welcome and nothing is 'weird' to ask.

questions.q: Who can you ask about puberty questions?
questions.a: A parent or guardian, doctor, school nurse or another trusted adult — or the anonymous question box.

days.guide: Watch the AMAZE video together, pausing to discuss. Your child lists changes that happen to everyone (growth spurt, body hair, more sweat and body odor, oily skin/acne, emotional changes).

questions.q: Name three changes that happen to everyone during puberty.
questions.a: Any three: growth spurt, new body hair (underarms, pubic area), more sweat/body odor, oilier skin and acne, stronger emotions/mood changes.

days.guide: Read that puberty usually starts between about 8 and 14. Your child writes 2–3 sentences on why comparing with friends isn't useful.

questions.q: Your friend has already grown 4 inches and you haven't. Is something wrong?
questions.a: No — each body follows its own timeline; starting earlier or later is normal.

days.guide: Your child graphs their height by year and looks for a steep part. Explain growth spurts (rapid height gain, bigger feet first) and that growing pains are aches in the legs, often at night.

questions.q: What is a growth spurt?
questions.a: A period of rapid growth in height (and weight), common during puberty.

days.guide: Pull questions from the box and answer them together calmly; it's fine to say 'Let me find out.' Then give the 5-question check orally.

questions.q: What starts puberty?
questions.a: Hormones — chemical messengers released when the brain (pituitary gland) signals the body to begin changing.

weeks.assessment_key: Quick check key: 1) Puberty = the time when the body develops from a child's into an adult's 2) Hormones start it 3) Usually begins about ages 8–14 4) Shared changes: growth spurt, body hair, sweat/odor, acne, emotions 5) Ask a trusted adult or valid source. Discussion: proficient if the child names at least one trusted adult and explains that different timelines are normal.

weeks.prep: Have the body map from week 2. Prepare a simple 'message-passing' game (folded notes passed from room to room). Preview the KidsHealth/AMAZE explanation of hormones in puberty. PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking hormones are only about moods. Hormones control growth, body changes and many body processes; moods are just one effect.
Thinking boys only have testosterone and girls only estrogen. Everyone has both; the amounts differ.

days.guide: Explain hormones as chemical messengers released by glands into the blood. Play a message game: you (the 'gland') send a note that travels by 'bloodstream' (hallway) to the target room.

questions.q: How do hormones travel through the body?
questions.a: Through the bloodstream to target organs.

days.guide: Add the pituitary gland to the body map. Explain it releases hormones that signal the ovaries or testes to make sex hormones.

questions.q: Why is the pituitary called the 'master gland'?
questions.a: It sends signals that control many other glands, including the ovaries and testes.

days.guide: Make a cause-and-effect chart: estrogen → breast development, wider hips, menstruation; testosterone → deeper voice, facial hair, muscle growth.

questions.q: Which hormone causes the voice to deepen?
questions.a: Testosterone.

days.guide: Read about mood changes; brainstorm coping strategies (exercise, talking, sleep, journaling).

questions.q: Give two healthy ways to deal with mood swings.
questions.a: Exercise, talking to a trusted adult, journaling, deep breathing, getting enough sleep.

days.guide: Draw a flowchart: brain/pituitary → hormones → ovaries/testes → estrogen/testosterone → body changes. Take the quiz.

questions.q: What are the glands that make sex hormones?
questions.a: Ovaries (estrogen) and testes (testosterone).

weeks.assessment_key: Flowchart: pituitary (in brain) → signals → ovaries or testes → estrogen or testosterone → physical changes. Quiz: 1) hormones = chemical messengers 2) travel in blood 3) pituitary = master gland 4) ovaries → estrogen 5) testes → testosterone 6) coping strategy. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Print labeled and blank diagrams of the female and male reproductive systems (KidsHealth or a health textbook). Preview AMAZE videos on reproductive anatomy. PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Using slang or nicknames for body parts. Correct names help when talking to doctors and keep kids safer.
Thinking the reproductive system is 'gross' or shameful. It's a normal body system like any other.

days.guide: Explain why correct names matter (clear communication with doctors and trusted adults, safety). Practice saying them matter-of-factly.

questions.q: Why is it important to use medically correct names?
questions.a: So you can communicate clearly with doctors and trusted adults about health or safety.

days.guide: Label the female diagram: ovaries (make eggs and estrogen), fallopian tubes (carry egg), uterus (where a baby can grow), vagina (birth canal).

questions.q: What is the function of the ovaries?
questions.a: To make eggs (ova) and the hormone estrogen.

days.guide: Label the male diagram: testes (make sperm and testosterone), scrotum (holds testes), penis, urethra.

questions.q: What is the function of the testes?
questions.a: To make sperm and the hormone testosterone.

days.guide: Create a T-chart of puberty changes in each system. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Give one change in each system during puberty.
questions.a: Female: ovaries begin releasing eggs, menstruation begins. Male: testes begin producing sperm.

days.guide: Diagram-labeling quiz; collect question-box questions. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Where does a fertilized egg develop into a baby?
questions.a: In the uterus.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram quiz: female — ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina; male — testes, scrotum, penis, urethra, sperm duct (vas deferens). Proficient = 80% labeled correctly with functions.

weeks.prep: Prepare a simple menstrual-cycle diagram (28-day circle) and optionally samples of pads, tampons, and period underwear. Preview AMAZE videos on periods and on erections/nocturnal emissions. PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking periods are dirty or a sign of illness. Menstruation is a normal, healthy part of the cycle.
Thinking wet dreams or erections mean something is wrong. They are normal and involuntary during puberty.

days.guide: Watch the video; draw a 28-day cycle: days ~1–5 menstruation, lining builds, ovulation around day 14, lining sheds if no pregnancy.

questions.q: What is menstruation?
questions.a: The monthly shedding of the uterine lining through the vagina when no pregnancy occurs.

days.guide: Learn about pads, tampons and period underwear; list items for a preparedness kit (pads, spare underwear, wipes, a small bag).

questions.q: What should go in a period-preparedness kit?
questions.a: Pads (or other products), spare underwear, wipes, and a small bag.

days.guide: Read about voice changes, erections and nocturnal emissions as normal. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is a nocturnal emission?
questions.a: Release of semen during sleep ('wet dream'); a normal, involuntary part of puberty.

days.guide: Write a hygiene plan for periods or for sweat, odor and shaving. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How often should pads be changed?
questions.a: Every 4–6 hours or as needed.

days.guide: Myth-or-fact quiz; discuss with a parent. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Myth or fact: You can't exercise during your period.
questions.a: Myth — exercise is fine and can even ease cramps.

weeks.assessment_key: Myth/fact key: Periods are normal — fact; Cycle is usually about 21–35 days (often ~28) — fact; You can't swim during a period — myth; Wet dreams are normal — fact; Voice cracks are temporary — fact; Only girls have hormones — myth. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print a feelings wheel and write scenario cards (two friendship scenarios, stereotype statements such as 'Boys don't cry' and 'Girls are bad at math'). Have the health journal ready. PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking strong or changing emotions mean something is wrong with you. Hormones and a developing brain make feelings more intense; this is normal and manageable.
Thinking a crush means you have to act on it or tell everyone. Crushes are normal feelings; you can keep them private and always treat others respectfully.
Treating stereotypes as facts. Statements about what all boys or all girls 'should' do are stereotypes; people vary.

days.guide: Show the feelings wheel; your child points to emotions they've felt lately (embarrassed, frustrated, excited, anxious). They write a paragraph about one: what caused it and what helped.

questions.q: Why might emotions feel stronger during puberty?
questions.a: Changing hormone levels and brain development make feelings more intense and can change quickly.

days.guide: Read two friendship-drift scenarios; your child applies the five decision steps to each. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Your best friend starts sitting with a new group. Name two healthy options.
questions.a: Talk to your friend honestly about how you feel; join the group or invite them to do something; also make new friends or join a club.

days.guide: Talk calmly about crushes as normal feelings. List respectful behaviors: kind words, no pressure, no teasing, and accepting 'no' immediately.

questions.q: If someone says 'no' or 'stop,' what should you do?
questions.a: Stop right away and respect their answer, without arguing or pressuring.

days.guide: Your child sorts statements into stereotype vs. fact and rewrites each stereotype respectfully.

questions.q: Is 'Boys don't cry' a fact or a stereotype? Rewrite it.
questions.a: A stereotype. Respectful version: 'Everyone has feelings, and crying is a normal way to express them.'

days.guide: Your child writes a journal entry about a coping strategy, then answers the check orally. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Name three healthy coping strategies for strong emotions.
questions.a: Any three: talk to a trusted adult or friend, exercise, deep breathing, journaling, drawing/music, taking a break, getting enough sleep.

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: 1) Emotions get stronger due to hormones/brain development — normal 2) a respectful response to a friendship change 3) 'no' means stop 4) identifies stereotypes vs. facts 5) names a trusted adult. Journal rubric: 4 = names a specific emotion, a realistic coping strategy and a trusted adult, with reflection on how it would help; 3 = strategy and emotion; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Prepare to have a 10-minute conversation with your child about puberty — decide what you're comfortable sharing from your own experience. Bookmark KidsHealth.org and AMAZE.org and find one random video comment section about puberty to compare. Review body-safety language: private parts, safe/unsafe touch, 'No, Go, Tell.' PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking parents don't want to talk about puberty. Most do; starting with a simple question helps.
Thinking secrets about touch should be kept if an adult asks. Unsafe touch or secrets about touch should always be told to a trusted adult; it's never the child's fault.

days.guide: Your child writes three conversation starters (e.g., 'What was puberty like for you?' 'Can I ask you something private?').

questions.q: Give a good conversation starter about puberty.
questions.a: Example: 'I learned about growth spurts today—when did yours happen?'

days.guide: Have the 10-minute talk using a starter. Your child records one thing they learned. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why is talking with a parent helpful?
questions.a: Parents can give accurate information, family values and support.

days.guide: Compare KidsHealth, AMAZE and a comment section on the same question; judge reliability. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why is a random video comment not a reliable source?
questions.a: Anyone can write it, with no medical expertise or fact-checking.

days.guide: Teach personal boundaries: your body belongs to you; safe vs. unsafe touch; if anyone makes you uncomfortable say No, Go, Tell.

questions.q: What should you do if someone touches you in an unsafe way?
questions.a: Say no, get away, and tell a trusted adult right away—and keep telling until someone helps.

days.guide: Make a pocket card of trusted adults and valid sources; role-play asking for help. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Name two valid sources of puberty information.
questions.a: KidsHealth.org, AMAZE.org, a doctor or school nurse.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play rubric: 4 = clearly states concern to a trusted adult, uses 'I' statements, asks for help, persists if not heard; 3 = clear but no persistence; 2 = vague; 1 = can't. Pocket card: at least 3 trusted adults and 2 valid sources (e.g., KidsHealth, AMAZE, doctor).

weeks.prep: Gather poster paper and markers. Write three fictional advice-column letters (e.g., 'I'm the shortest in my class,' 'I sweat a lot,' 'My friend teases me about my voice'). PARENT PREVIEW: watch the videos and read materials before your child does; decide how you'll answer personal or values questions, and keep the anonymous question box open.
misconceptions: Thinking teasing about development is harmless. It hurts and is a form of bullying.
Thinking a self-care kit is only for girls. Everyone benefits from deodorant, a spare shirt and tissues.

days.guide: Build a concept map linking hormones → physical changes → emotions → hygiene → trusted adults.

questions.q: How are hormones connected to hygiene needs?
questions.a: Hormones make sweat and oil glands more active, so you need to shower, use deodorant and wash your face more often.

days.guide: Role-play responding to teasing about early or late development. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What's a good response if someone teases you about developing late?
questions.a: Stay calm, say 'Everyone grows at their own pace,' walk away, and tell an adult if it continues.

days.guide: List or assemble a self-care kit: deodorant, tissues, wipes, spare shirt/underwear, pads if needed, lip balm, comb.

questions.q: Name four items for a self-care kit.
questions.a: Deodorant, tissues, spare underwear/shirt, wipes, pads, comb, water bottle.

days.guide: Answer three advice-column letters with kind, accurate advice. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Answer: 'I'm the shortest in my class—is something wrong?'
questions.a: Probably not—puberty and growth spurts start at different ages; many people catch up. Talk to your doctor if worried.

days.guide: Take the unit test and discuss results. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Which gland signals puberty to begin?
questions.a: The pituitary gland.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) puberty starts ~8–14 2) pituitary gland 3) estrogen and testosterone 4) ovaries make eggs, testes make sperm 5) menstruation = shedding uterine lining 6) nocturnal emissions are normal 7) hygiene: shower, deodorant 8) emotions change, coping strategies 9) trusted adults and valid sources 10) respect and no teasing. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather straws (thin coffee stirrers work best), a jar with cotton balls (to show tar), and a body diagram. Read the CDC or NIDA for Teens fact sheet on tobacco.
misconceptions: Thinking smoking only harms lungs. It harms the heart, blood vessels, mouth, teeth, skin and nearly every organ.
Thinking you can't get addicted from 'just a few.' Teen brains get addicted to nicotine faster than adult brains.

days.guide: Read about nicotine (addictive drug), tar (sticky residue that coats lungs) and carbon monoxide (poison gas that reduces oxygen in blood). Label the body diagram with effects.

questions.q: What does carbon monoxide do in the body?
questions.a: It replaces oxygen in the blood, so less oxygen reaches the body's organs and muscles.

days.guide: Jog in place 1 minute, then breathe only through a thin straw for 30 seconds (stop at once if dizzy). Write a reflection.

questions.q: What did the straw activity model?
questions.a: How damaged lungs or narrowed airways from smoking make it hard to breathe.

days.guide: Explain nicotine triggers dopamine in the reward system; the brain starts craving it. Teen brains are still developing, so addiction happens faster.

questions.q: Why do teens get addicted to nicotine faster than adults?
questions.a: The teen brain is still developing and is more sensitive to nicotine's effects on the reward system.

days.guide: Research secondhand smoke (causes asthma attacks, ear infections, lung problems in non-smokers) and CA laws (tobacco sales age 21, smoke-free workplaces, restaurants and parks).

questions.q: What is secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Smoke breathed in by people near someone smoking.

days.guide: Tobacco-effects quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Name three harmful substances in cigarette smoke.
questions.a: Nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide (also many other chemicals).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) nicotine = addictive drug 2) tar coats lungs 3) CO reduces oxygen in blood 4) teens get addicted faster 5) secondhand smoke harms others 6) CA legal age for tobacco = 21 7) effects: heart disease, lung cancer, stained teeth, bad breath. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Download the FDA or CDC 'E-cigarettes/vaping' fact sheet for youth. Write 10 vaping statements on cards (myths and facts). Find recent youth vaping survey data (National Youth Tobacco Survey: in recent years roughly 9 in 10 middle and high schoolers do NOT vape) and images of vape packaging from a news or health site.
misconceptions: Thinking vape aerosol is 'just water vapor.' It contains nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals and metals like nickel and lead.
Thinking 'everyone vapes.' Survey data show most youth do not vape.

days.guide: Read the fact sheet; your child lists what's in vape aerosol. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name three things found in vape aerosol.
questions.a: Nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals (like diacetyl), volatile organic compounds, heavy metals (nickel, tin, lead).

days.guide: Sort 10 statements into myths and facts with evidence from the sheet. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Myth or fact: Vapes are safe because they don't burn tobacco.
questions.a: Myth — vape aerosol still contains nicotine and harmful chemicals that damage lungs and the developing brain.

days.guide: Look at packaging images; discuss bright colors, candy and fruit flavors, cartoon designs.

questions.q: How do flavors and packaging target young people?
questions.a: Sweet candy/fruit flavors and bright, fun packaging appeal to kids and make vaping seem harmless.

days.guide: Make a bar graph from survey data showing most youth don't vape. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why does knowing the real norm help?
questions.a: It shows that not vaping is normal, which reduces pressure to try it.

days.guide: Write a 30–60 second PSA script correcting one myth. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What should a strong PSA include?
questions.a: A clear message, an accurate fact from a valid source, and a call to action.

weeks.assessment_key: PSA rubric: 4 = names a specific myth, corrects it with an accurate fact from a valid source (FDA/CDC), engaging delivery and a clear call to action; 3 = accurate correction but no source or call to action; 2 = vague or partly inaccurate; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Find historical cigarette ads (Stanford Research into the Impact of Tobacco Advertising collection) and modern vape ads/social media images. Write 4 refusal role-play scenarios (older kid at the park offers a vape; friend at a sleepover; cousin; online).
misconceptions: Thinking saying no means losing friends. Real friends respect your choices; you can suggest another activity.
Confusing assertive with aggressive. Assertive is firm and respectful; aggressive is hostile.

days.guide: Compare old cigarette ads with today's vape marketing; identify techniques (celebrity, glamour, doctors, flavors, freedom).

questions.q: What technique did old cigarette ads use by showing doctors?
questions.a: Health claims/authority (testimonial) to suggest smoking was safe.

days.guide: Teach refusal steps: say no clearly, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Give an example of a complete refusal.
questions.a: 'No thanks, I don't vape. It's bad for my lungs. Let's go shoot hoops instead.' Then walk away if needed.

days.guide: Role-play the 4 scenarios; switch roles. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What if they keep pressuring you?
questions.a: Repeat 'no' firmly (broken record) and leave.

days.guide: Demonstrate passive, aggressive and assertive tone and body language. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Describe assertive body language.
questions.a: Stand tall, eye contact, calm firm voice.

days.guide: Perform a refusal role-play and take the unit test. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Why is nicotine harmful to young people?
questions.a: It is highly addictive and harms the developing brain (attention, learning, impulse control).

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play rubric (1–4 each): clear 'no', reason, alternative, assertive voice/body, walks away if needed. Unit test key: nicotine addictive, tar, CO, vape aerosol contents, flavors target youth, most teens don't vape, secondhand smoke, refusal steps, legal age 21. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather a body diagram; optionally clear a safe space for the spinning coordination demo. Read a NIDA/KidsHealth article on alcohol's effects.
misconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant because people get loud. Alcohol is a depressant: it slows the brain and nervous system.
Thinking only heavy drinking is harmful for kids. Any alcohol is harmful to a developing brain, and it's illegal under 21.

days.guide: Trace alcohol's path: mouth → stomach and small intestine → bloodstream → brain (slows thinking, coordination) and liver (breaks it down).

questions.q: Which organ breaks down alcohol?
questions.a: The liver.

days.guide: Spin 5 times then try to walk a line (with a spotter, on soft ground). Discuss how alcohol similarly impairs balance and coordination.

questions.q: How does alcohol affect coordination and reaction time?
questions.a: It slows the brain's signals, so balance, coordination and reaction time get worse.

days.guide: Read why alcohol harms the developing brain (memory, learning, decision-making); the brain develops into the mid-20s; legal age is 21.

questions.q: Why is the legal drinking age 21?
questions.a: The brain is still developing, alcohol can damage it, and young drinkers are at higher risk of accidents and addiction.

days.guide: Make a short- vs. long-term chart. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Give one short-term and one long-term effect.
questions.a: Short: slowed reactions, poor judgment, vomiting. Long: liver disease, brain damage, addiction.

days.guide: Alcohol facts quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Is alcohol a stimulant or depressant?
questions.a: A depressant.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) depressant 2) liver breaks it down 3) bloodstream carries it to the brain 4) impairs coordination, judgment, reaction time 5) legal age 21 6) brain develops until mid-20s 7) long-term: liver disease, addiction, brain damage. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Read NIDA for Teens articles on marijuana and inhalants. Gather household product labels (spray paint, glue, aerosol cleaner) to read warnings — do NOT open or sniff them. Save the Poison Control number (1-800-222-1222).
misconceptions: Thinking cannabis is harmless because it's legal for adults in California. It's illegal under 21 and can harm memory, learning and reaction time in young people.
Thinking household products are safe because they're sold in stores. Sniffing them can cause sudden death even the first time.

days.guide: Read the NIDA article; your child lists effects on memory, learning and reaction time. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What chemical in cannabis causes its effects?
questions.a: THC.

days.guide: Discuss edibles that look like candy or cookies; if found, don't eat, tell an adult, call Poison Control if eaten.

questions.q: What should you do if you find a candy that might be an edible?
questions.a: Don't eat it; leave it and tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Read warning labels; explain that inhalant fumes can cause 'sudden sniffing death' (heart failure) and brain damage.

questions.q: Why are inhalants so dangerous?
questions.a: They can cause the heart to fail suddenly, even the first time, and damage the brain.

days.guide: Learn CA law (cannabis illegal under 21) and data showing most youth don't use it. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How old must you be to legally use cannabis in California?

days.guide: Matching quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Match: THC, inhalant, edible.
questions.a: THC = active chemical in cannabis; inhalant = fumes sniffed from household products; edible = cannabis in food.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching key: THC → chemical in cannabis that affects the brain; edible → food containing cannabis, can look like candy; inhalant → household product fumes; sudden sniffing death → heart failure from inhalants; Poison Control → 1-800-222-1222; legal age → 21. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Get an empty OTC medicine box with a Drug Facts label (e.g., children's acetaminophen) and a prescription label (or an example). Check your home medicine storage beforehand. Write down Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.
misconceptions: Thinking OTC medicines are always safe because no prescription is needed. Wrong doses can be dangerous.
Sharing prescriptions. A prescription is for one person only.

days.guide: Compare a prescription label (name, dose, doctor, pharmacy, refills) and Drug Facts label (active ingredient, uses, warnings, directions).

questions.q: What does 'active ingredient' mean?
questions.a: The part of the medicine that works on the body.

days.guide: Use a dose chart for 3 problems by age/weight. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: A chart says ages 6–11: 1 tablet every 4–6 hours, max 5 in 24 hours. What's the most you can take in a day?
questions.a: 5 tablets.

days.guide: Discuss why sharing prescriptions or extra doses is dangerous. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why is taking double doses dangerous?
questions.a: Too much can cause overdose and organ damage.

days.guide: Inspect home medicine storage; learn Poison Control number. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What's the Poison Control number?

days.guide: Medicine-safety scenario quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Who should give you medicine?
questions.a: A parent, guardian or trusted adult, following directions.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: never take medicine without a trusted adult; follow directions; don't share prescriptions; store safely; call Poison Control. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Make a wallet-card template. Look up your local resources (pediatrician, school or co-op counselor). Key numbers: 911 (emergency), Poison Control 1-800-222-1222, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text). Al-Anon/Alateen supports young people affected by someone else's drinking. Find a short story or KidsHealth article about a child whose parent drinks too much. PARENT PREVIEW: if your family has experienced addiction, read the story first and be ready for questions.
misconceptions: Thinking a family member's drinking or drug use is the child's fault, or that the child can fix it. It is never the child's fault; adults are responsible for getting help.
Thinking telling an adult about a vape or pills will get you or a friend 'in trouble.' Telling keeps people safe; trusted adults want to know.

days.guide: Your child lists trusted adults and community resources for drug concerns (parent, doctor, school counselor, Poison Control, faith leader, relative).

questions.q: Who would you call if a younger sibling swallowed pills from a cabinet?
questions.a: Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away (911 if the child is unconscious, having trouble breathing, or having a seizure), and tell a parent.

days.guide: Read the story; ask how the child feels (confused, embarrassed, worried) and where they could get support.

questions.q: Name two places a kid can get support when a family member has an alcohol problem.
questions.a: Any two: a trusted adult (relative, teacher), school counselor, doctor, Alateen, faith leader.

days.guide: Your child writes a short script: 'I need to tell you something. I found ___ at ___. I'm worried. Can you help?' Practice saying it.

questions.q: What three things should your script include?
questions.a: What you found or saw, where/when, and a clear request for help.

days.guide: Design a wallet-size card with 911, Poison Control, 988, and two trusted adults' numbers. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: When do you call 911 instead of Poison Control?
questions.a: When someone is unconscious, not breathing, having a seizure, or in immediate danger.

days.guide: Give the Alcohol and Other Drugs unit test. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do if you find pills or a vape?
questions.a: Don't touch or use it; tell a trusted adult right away.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) alcohol is a depressant 2) liver breaks it down 3) legal age for alcohol and cannabis in CA = 21 4) THC is the active chemical in cannabis 5) edibles may look like candy—don't eat, tell an adult 6) inhalants can cause sudden death even first time 7) OTC vs. prescription differences 8) never share prescriptions 9) Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 10) tell a trusted adult. Proficient = 80% or better.

weeks.prep: Print an influence web template (you in the center; family, friends, media, culture, community around). Write 6 peer-pressure scenarios (spoken, unspoken, online). Find an alcohol ad (magazine or online) to analyze.
misconceptions: Thinking peer pressure is always spoken. Unspoken pressure (everyone doing something) and online pressure are powerful too.
Thinking all influences are negative. Family rules, coaches, and goals are positive influences (protective factors).

days.guide: Your child completes the influence web, noting positive and negative influences on decisions about drugs.

questions.q: Give one positive and one negative influence on decisions about drugs.
questions.a: Positive: family rules, a coach, friends who don't use. Negative: ads that glamorize drinking, older kids who vape.

days.guide: Your child labels 6 scenarios as spoken, unspoken or online pressure. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Everyone at a party is vaping, but no one asks you. What kind of pressure is that?
questions.a: Unspoken peer pressure.

days.guide: Analyze an alcohol ad: who is it targeting, what does it suggest, what does it leave out? Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What do alcohol ads usually leave out?
questions.a: Health risks, addiction, impaired driving, hangovers, and that it's illegal under 21.

days.guide: List protective factors in your child's life and how each helps. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a protective factor?
questions.a: Something in your life that lowers the chance of risky behavior, like strong family relationships, activities, goals or supportive friends.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on the strongest influence and how to respond. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How can you respond to a negative influence?
questions.a: Recognize it, think about your values and goals, use refusal skills, and choose friends who support you.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = names the strongest influence, explains how it affects choices with an example, and gives a specific healthy response; 3 = names and explains; 2 = names only; 1 = missing.
